deep.reconstruction:
Context. On the previous page Hilbert treats functions of the coefficients u_ik of an n-ary quadratic form phi(v) = sum u_ik v_i v_k. These functions are invariant under the substitutions v -> g v with g in GL_n(Z), which induce substitutions of the u_ik (u -> g^T u g). His points are:
- Such substitutions are either of finitely many generating types or parabolic. In the parabolic case the form can be brought to uw - v^2, with u'=u, v'=v+u, w'=w+2v+u.
- The locus where the u_ik are real (or have real ratios) carries the parabolic points.
- A third case occurs only on the discriminant locus U=0.
- One should construct the 'Urbereich' (fundamental domain, the reduced space of quadratic forms) and the generators of the group 'exactly by Poincaré's method'.

This page.

(a) Lines 1-4. The sentence finishes: '(cf. my lecture course on single-valued functions with transformations into themselves)'. Conversely he wants to interpret and exploit Minkowski's methods (generalised notions of length and volume, i.e. the geometry of numbers / reduction theory) for these questions. This is a research programme: join Poincaré's automorphic-function machinery with Minkowski's reduction theory.

(b) The main note. Besides the quadratic-form case (implicitly f = sum 1/phi(v)^s, an Epstein-type series), one can study
  f(u; s) = sum_{v in Z^n \ 0} 1/psi(v)^s,
where psi is first a bilinear form. Above all he takes psi to be a decomposable form, a product of n linear forms:
  psi(v) = prod_{i=1}^n (u_i1 v_1 + ... + u_in v_n) = prod_i (u v)_i.
Then f is viewed as a function of the n^2 complex variables u_11..u_nn, which 'are to be transformed simultaneously in a certain way'.

The implicit invariance (my filling): replacing v by g v with g in GL_n(Z) permutes Z^n \ 0. Hence f(u g) = f(u), i.e. f is invariant under right multiplication of the matrix u by GL_n(Z). This acts simultaneously on all rows (all n linear forms). In addition there is the obvious invariance under permuting the rows. It is also invariant under scaling rows by factors whose product is 1, provided the branch of ^s is handled.

He then asserts two things:
- A fundamental domain ('Urbereich') exists 'for the same reasons as before'.
- Convergence of the series is always to be inferred as in Poincaré (Poincaré-series convergence arguments), 'where one may possibly have to transform the variables'.

An isolated cancelled mark follows. The page is a programme sketch; no computation is carried out.
errors: The convergence claim is unjustified as stated and false in general. For real u (or u coming from a totally real number field), the decomposable form prod_i L_i(v) is constant on orbits of the unit group (or takes arbitrarily small values on lattice points). The sum over all v in Z^n\0 then diverges. Hecke's later remedy is to sum over v modulo units (or over ideals).

For complex u with n >= 3, each complex linear form, viewed as a real map R^n -> C, has a kernel of real dimension >= n-2 > 0. Lattice points close to that kernel make |psi(v)| small, so absolute convergence of the full lattice sum is not guaranteed. Poincaré's argument for Fuchsian/theta series does not transfer automatically. (For n=2 with generic complex u each L_i is injective on R^2, so |psi(v)| >= c|v|^2 and the series converges for Re s > 1.)

The existence of a fundamental domain for GL_n(Z) acting on the n^2-dimensional complex space of u (decomposable forms) is merely asserted by analogy with the quadratic-form case. In the full complex space the action is far from properly discontinuous without restricting to a suitable domain. This is a heuristic, not a proof.
Minor slip in the formula: 'u_12 u_2' should read 'u_12 v_2'.

results.what: Programme to combine Poincaré's theory of automorphic functions (fundamental domain, generators, convergence of Poincaré series) with Minkowski's geometry of numbers / reduction theory for the action of GL_n(Z) on spaces of forms.
results.modern_name: Reduction theory and automorphic forms for arithmetic groups (GL_n(Z) acting on the space of positive forms; Siegel/Borel–Harish-Chandra programme)

results.what: Dirichlet series f(u;s) = sum over integer vectors of psi(v)^(-s), with psi a quadratic/bilinear form, regarded as an automorphic function of the form's coefficients.
results.modern_name: Epstein zeta function / Eisenstein series on GL_n
results.usually_credited_to: Epstein (1903); Eisenstein-series viewpoint: Maass, Selberg, Langlands

results.what: Lattice sum of the inverse s-th power of a decomposable (norm-type) form prod_i (u v)_i, as a function of n^2 complex variables transformed simultaneously, i.e. invariant under u -> u g, g in GL_n(Z).
results.modern_name: Zeta functions of decomposable/norm forms (Hecke zeta functions); relatedly Hilbert modular functions with simultaneous action on several variables, and Shintani zeta functions
results.usually_credited_to: Hecke (1917-20) for norm-form zeta functions; Blumenthal (1903) for Hilbert modular functions, building on Hilbert's ideas

deep.surprise_reason: It is known that Hilbert in his Königsberg period thought about automorphic functions in several variables (the origin of Hilbert modular functions, passed to Blumenthal). It is also known that he followed Poincaré and Minkowski closely. A note proposing Epstein-type Dirichlet series and lattice sums of decomposable forms as automorphic functions of the form's coefficients, linked explicitly to Minkowski's methods, is a notable unpublished anticipation of ideas later associated with Epstein, Hecke and Eisenstein series on GL_n. However, it is only a sketch, with unjustified (partly incorrect) convergence claims.
